World.title: Romania to take over rotating presidency of the South-East European Cooperation Process
World.content:
Romania is set to take over the Presidency of the South-East European Cooperation Process (SEECP) between July 2026 and June 2027 during the summit taking place in Sofia, according to the Ministry of Foreign Affairs.

Romania’s mandate at the SEECP Presidency will have three priorities, namely supporting the EU enlargement process and the gradual integration of participants into the European Single Market; strengthening resilience against hybrid and cyber threats, disinformation, as well as natural disasters and medical emergencies; and the implementation of the SEE 2030 Strategy and the Green Agenda for the Western Balkans, with a special focus on youth and civil society.

The SEECP meeting in the Bulgarian capital will be attended by acting foreign minister Oana Țoiu, on behalf of president Nicușor Dan.

The event marks 30 years since the establishment of the format and the conclusion of the Bulgarian presidency, but also the beginning of the Romanian presidency.

“The overlap of the presidency year with the period of negotiations for the future multiannual EU budget will allow us a greater focus on strategic projects for connecting the EU with the region, with Romania being a direct beneficiary of these projects,” Oana Țoiu said in the press release.

The official also said that Romania is a partner for countries in the region on the path to adapting to European standards. The region is at a “key moment,” transitioning from being perceived as an unstable one to one with growth potential, according to Țoiu.

SEECP is the only cooperation forum in South-East Europe created and managed by participants from the region. The organization was launched in 1996 at the initiative of Bulgaria. Founding members include Albania, Bosnia and Herzegovina, Bulgaria, Greece, North Macedonia, Romania, Serbia, and Turkey. Croatia, Moldova, Montenegro, Slovenia, and Kosovo joined later.

Romania has previously held three mandates at the helm of SEECP between March 1999 and March 2000, April 2004 and May 2005, and July 2013 and June 2014.

World.title: Serbian Police Unit Members Arrested Over Alleged Cover-Up of Restaurant Shooting
World.content:
Serbian police on Wednesday arrested a police unit commander, his deputy and other two members of Intervention Unit 92, a specialised police unit in Belgrade, over a shooting in a city restaurant in November, which the prosecution suspects they tried to cover up.

The unit commander, identified only as D.N., and his deputy, J.S., were arrested on suspicion of influence peddling in co-perpetration, the Higher Prosecutor’s Office said in a press release. Intervention Unit members N.S. and N.K. were arrested on suspicion of abuse of official position.

The manager of the restaurant where the shooting occurred, named only as D.Z., was arrested on suspicion of failure to report a crime and its perpetrator, and of assisting the perpetrator after the commission of a crime.

One suspect is still being sought.

Another suspect, named as S.V., is under investigation for endangering public safety and illegal possession and carrying of weapons. The Higher Prosecutor’s Office said he is already in detention on suspicion of attempted aggravated murder.

Although it is not explicitly mentioned, someone with those initials is already in detention as the alleged killer in a murder case in another Belgrade restaurant, in which former Belgrade police chief Veselin Milic was arrested and detained.

The prosecution said it believes S.V. became involved in a fight in a restaurant and fired a shot in the direction of a person nicknamed “Runjo”. He did not hit him but the bullet struck the glass in the restaurant.

The commander of the police unit and his deputy then allegedly hatched an agreement about how to persuade their subordinates, N.S. and N.K., not to investigate the incident.

They allegedly told N.S. and N.K. “which actions they should not take, namely not to inform the crime scene investigation team, not to secure the crime scene for the purpose of conducting an investigation, not to carry out an investigation and collect evidence for the committed criminal offence, not to notify the competent public prosecutor’s office about the incident, and to present the event as a verbal argument and an ordinary bar fight”, the prosecution said.

The manager of the restaurant allegedly failed to report to the police that a shooting had occurred, even though he had been personally present. The prosecution claims he then concealed evidence by deleting surveillance camera footage, instructing employees to clean the crime scene in order to hide evidence, and told the police that the hole in the glass caused by the shooting had existed previously.

Former Belgrade police chief Veselin Milic was arrested on May 15 on suspicion of assisting an offender after the commission of the crime of aggravated murder in another Belgrade restaurant. This criminal complaint was dropped by the Higher Prosecutor’s Office on Tuesday. However. Milic still faces allegations that he failed to report a crime.

As part of the same case, two police officers of Serbia’s Witness Protection Unit were arrested and questioned last week.

Media have reported that the victim of the restaurant shooting was a gangland figure, but this has not been confirmed officially.

After Milic’s arrest, President Aleksandar Vucic announced the adoption of a law under which any police officer or soldier caught performing other jobs, beyond those directly permitted by the state, will no longer be able to work in any part of the police or armed forces.

“It’s very important to show zero tolerance toward those who collaborate with drug dealers and criminals,” Vucic said on May 20.

World.title: Gamechanger? Bosnia’s World Cup Participation Could Create Moment of Collective Pride
World.content:
Post-war institutional and identity politics have been reflected in the situation of the Bosnian football team. In 2011, Bosnia and Herzegovina was suspended by FIFA and UEFA because its football association had failed to adopt statutes compatible with international rules. The issue became widely associated with Bosnia’s ethnocratic governance culture, including the logic of collective and ethnically “balanced” leadership rather than a professional and merit-based functional institutional structure.

The suspension was lifted only after reforms were introduced. In that sense, the football association had become a miniature version of Bosnia’s political system – shared on paper but sabotaged by competing ethno-nationalist political narratives and by the difficulty of building normal institutions in a divided constitutional order.

Even today, the national team is not supported equally by everyone in Bosnia. Its strongest emotional base is among Bosniaks and those who identify simply as Bosnians. But many Bosnian Croats, Serbs and others also support the national team, even if that support is uneven, situational or mixed with other loyalties.

Bosnia is full of layered identities and football reflects that reality. People may feel attached at once to a local club, to Bosnia, to Croatia or Serbia, and even to Yugoslav nostalgia and memories, or to a wider regional identification regarding the Balkans.

Across the former Yugoslav space, people still follow one another’s teams, artists and public figures more closely than formal politics would suggest. Eurovision is one example. In football the former Yugoslav space remains politically divided, but socially and emotionally more entangled than nationalist narratives usually admit.

Bosnia’s qualification is also connected to experiences of migration during and after the war. The national team reflects the country’s modern demographic reality; according to some recent estimates the country has a relatively small resident population while large numbers of people born in Bosnia, or descended from Bosnian families, live in Europe and other parts of the world.

This means the national team represents more than a state within its borders. It also represents a transnational experience since several players were born outside Bosnia or spent most of their lives abroad. In that sense, the team mirrors the country’s post-war migration, economic weakness and demographic decline. At the same time, it also shows how diaspora links can sustain identification with Bosnia even when everyday life takes place elsewhere.

Bosnia’s participation in the World Cup will not solve its constitutional, structural, institutional or many other problems. It does not remove corruption, constitutional deadlock or the long habit of political division. But it can still matter politically in a broader sense.

In a country moving toward another election period, World Cup participation offers something rare based on positive energy and experiences instead of fear, exclusion or grievance.

It creates a moment in which success is shared more widely than usual. Football in Bosnia has almost always contained both unity and division, depending on the historical context and the political level. That is why this qualification matters; it reminds that in Bosnia, shared public emotion is still possible, even in a country built around division.

Vladan Lausevic is a writer and social entrepreneur based in Stockholm, Sweden.
